title: The email you keep not sending: write, send, follow up
dek: Write the request before the background, check the facts and recipient, then choose a follow-up date that reflects the actual deadline.
metaDescription: Start an avoided email with a concrete request, use a short send check, and follow up without invented waiting rules or promises of a reply.

paragraphs: Start the email you keep not sending by writing what the recipient needs to do, know or decide. Add only the facts needed for that purpose, check the recipient and attachments, then send. Record a follow-up date based on the actual deadline or stated response time, not a universal rule about how many days politeness requires.

A draft can grow while the request remains missing. You add the history, soften the opening and explain the delay, but still have not asked for the appointment date or corrected invoice. Work on that sentence first. This guide covers ordinary correspondence, not formal service of notices, emergency reporting or legal submissions.

body.heading: Start with the job of the message

items.line: Please confirm [specific fact] for [reference or context] by [date, if relevant]. I need it to [brief practical reason].
On [date], I noticed [observable problem]. Please confirm the reporting process and the next step. I have included [relevant evidence].
I have not replied sooner. My answer is [answer]. The next step I can take is [specific action and realistic date].
Thank you for asking. I cannot [request]. I wanted to confirm that so you can make other arrangements.

body.heading: Invented example: the ask comes before the history
paragraphs: A fictional customer needs an invoice corrected before submitting an expense claim on Friday. The subject is 'Invoice 482: please confirm corrected address by Thursday.' The first line is 'Please send a corrected invoice showing [correct address], or confirm what you need from me to amend it.' The customer then gives the invoice date and points to the incorrect field.

The message does not include every earlier purchase or an accusation about why the mistake happened. It does include the real expense deadline as context, without pretending that the recipient has already agreed to Thursday. If the deadline is not feasible, the customer asks for an alternative plan.

body.heading: Check once for concrete errors
items: Put the request, answer or decision near the start.
Confirm the recipient is the right person or official reporting address.
Include a relevant reference and accurate dates without unnecessary personal information.
Attach the intended file and check it is the correct version.
Distinguish a deadline you must meet from a response date you are requesting.
Remove claims about motives, promises or earlier conversations you cannot support.
Choose a follow-up date and record where the sent message will be found.

body.heading: Choose follow-up timing from the situation
paragraphs: If the organization publishes a response period, use it as one input while also considering your own deadline. If someone promised an answer Tuesday, a check after that missed commitment may be appropriate. If there is no stated timeframe, choose a reasonable date for this specific task and record why. There is no single five-day or ten-day schedule for every message.

The [BBC Office English discussion](https://downloads.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/office_english/240205_OfficeEnglish_ChasingPeople_Transcript_.pdf) offers examples of reminder language and increasing clarity. It is language guidance, not evidence that a particular phrase or channel produces faster replies. The scripts here are original starting points, not guaranteed persuasion.

Keep follow-ups in the existing thread when useful so the recipient can see the request and evidence. Change channel if the published process, urgency or repeated delivery problem calls for it. A phone call is not automatically better: some matters require a portal or written notice to create the right record.

items.line: I am following up on my message of [date] about [specific request]. Can you confirm whether it reached the right team and when I should expect a response?
You mentioned a response by [date]. I have not received it. Please confirm the next step and revised expected date, or tell me what is still needed from me.
I need [specific item] for [real deadline]. If it cannot be provided by then, please tell me what alternative route or interim evidence is available.

body.heading: Know when not to wait for email
paragraphs: Do not use ordinary email for an immediate safety issue or urgent medical concern. Use the appropriate urgent service or designated reporting route. For legal, contractual or complaint deadlines, verify the required method and do not assume a sent email satisfies it or pauses the deadline.

Before adding another recipient, consider confidentiality and whether they actually own the next step. Avoid copying a wider group merely to create pressure. Keep the escalation factual: dates, request, responses and the outcome needed. If the situation is disputed or high-stakes, obtain suitable advice rather than escalating through increasingly forceful wording.

If sending itself remains difficult, save the request sentence as a first step and schedule a short return. For a consequential deadline, ask someone to help check the message now. Persistent difficulty handling messages may warrant broader support; one writing template cannot explain or treat its cause.

items.q: How long should I wait before chasing an email?
items.a: Use the actual deadline, the recipient's stated response period and any promised date. When none exists, choose a proportionate check-back date for that task. Do not apply an etiquette rule that risks a real deadline, and do not assume repeated same-day reminders will help.

items.q: Should I apologize for following up?
items.a: A routine follow-up does not need an apology just for existing. Acknowledge a delay you caused when relevant, then make the request clear. There is no useful apology quota; accuracy, proportion and the relationship matter more than counting how often you say sorry.

items.q: What if I receive another vague update?
items.a: Ask what concrete step remains, who owns it and when a response is expected. A date is useful planning information, not a guarantee. If the process is failing, check the official escalation route and keep the message history rather than endlessly rewriting the same request.
